glossary.definition: Total addressable market is all the spending in the market you describe; the serviceable available market is the part you can reach; the serviceable obtainable market is the part you can realistically win.
How quantity demanded changes as price changes; its slope and the elasticity at the mean are what the demand tool reports.
The percentage change in quantity demanded for a one-percent change in price; above one in absolute value is elastic, below one is inelastic.
What survey respondents say they will buy, weighted into an expected buying rate; a statement of intent, not a record of purchases.
Customer acquisition cost: what you spend, on average, to win one customer.
Customer lifetime value: the contribution a customer brings over their life; here, margin divided by the declared churn rate.
The share of customers who stop buying each period, entered as a decimal (5% is 0.05).
The share of a cohort still buying in a later period; its complement is churn.
A group of customers who started in the same period, followed together over later periods.
Price minus variable cost per unit: what each sale leaves towards fixed costs and profit.
The ordered stages a customer passes through, from first contact to purchase, with the count at each stage.
The share of the people at one stage who reach the next stage, or the share of visitors who complete the desired action.
The share of free trials that become paying customers, measured over a declared window.
Click-through rate: clicks divided by impressions.
Cost per click: advertising spend divided by clicks.
Cost per thousand impressions: spend divided by impressions, multiplied by 1,000.
Cost per acquisition: spend divided by the number of customers or actions won.
Return on ad spend: revenue attributed to the campaign divided by the spend.
Advertising cost of sales: spend divided by revenue, the inverse of ROAS, expressed as a percentage.
The ROAS at which campaign revenue exactly covers spend after the contribution margin: 1 / contribution margin ratio.
The rule that decides which touchpoint receives credit for a conversion; first-click, last-click, linear and position-based rules give different answers.
The conversions that would not have happened without the campaign; a causal question that attribution credit alone cannot answer.
The tagging convention (source, medium, campaign, content, term) that lets analytics group visits by where they came from.
Search engine optimisation: earning unpaid search traffic by making pages relevant and technically sound.
Search engine marketing: paid search advertising, usually charged per click.
Conversion-rate optimisation: changing a page or journey and testing whether the completion rate really improved.
A controlled comparison of two versions, where the difference in outcomes is tested against the range chance alone could produce.
The chance a test detects a real effect of a declared size; it sets the sample you need before you start.
Marketing-qualified lead and sales-qualified lead: two declared stages a lead passes before it becomes an opportunity.
How the budget is divided across channels, and the evidence for what each channel returns.
Recency, frequency and monetary value: three transaction-based measures used to group customers by buying behaviour.
Classifies product attributes by how their presence or absence affects satisfaction, from must-be to attractive.
A service-quality instrument that compares customer expectations with perceptions across declared dimensions.
A one-to-five band given by ranking the customers in your own file into five equal-count groups; the top band is five, and recency is ranked in reverse.
A label taken from a declared grid of recency, frequency and monetary scores, such as Champions or At risk; the label describes buying behaviour in one snapshot.
The number of people who see a vehicle at least once in the period, counted once each however many times they see it.
Reach divided by the declared target population, expressed as a decimal (45% is 0.45).
The average number of times a reached person sees the message; for a plan it is gross impressions divided by combined reach.
Reach multiplied by average frequency: a count of exposures, not of people.
Gross rating points: reach share times average frequency times one hundred. Points add up across vehicles; people do not.
Cost per rating point: cost divided by gross rating points, the price of one percent of the population seeing one insertion.
The combined number of different people a set of vehicles reaches; estimated here by the random-duplication formula, so it is an upper bound.
The firm's sales divided by the total sales of the declared market, over the same period and in the same currency.
The share of the declared target population that buys; it counts buyers once, however often they buy.
The firm's sales divided by the largest declared competitor's sales; above one means the firm is the leader.
The margin a customer is expected to leave over a declared horizon, discounted to today and reduced each period by churn.
The per-period rate used to bring a future amount back to today; a higher rate makes future margin worth less.
How few segments produce a declared share of the total profit, read from the segments ranked by profit.

people.label: People & organisation
people.summary: Design the job, develop the people who do it, and read the organisation they work in.
start_steps: Name the decision you are taking: the job, the training, the team, the change or the design.
Open the tile that holds it and read what the framework needs before you start.
Write the brief: what you know, what you have observed and what you want the paper to settle.
Check the evidence on every part and add your own where the pipeline found nothing.
Read the limitations before you cite it: each framework here states what it cannot settle.
does_not: The reward tile is empty because no reward or job-evaluation framework is in the catalogue.

It does not compute headcount, turnover, absence, cost per hire, time to hire, compa-ratio, span of control, diversity, engagement or a nine-box score: the frozen core has no such method, and a similar method is not a substitute for it.
The frameworks here record and evidence a decision; they do not design the role, run the training, choose the intervention or predict who will succeed.
A catalogue-only framework is something to read and cite. It is not a worksheet until the owner builds one.
people.guidance: Start with the tile that matches the decision. Strategy and design covers how the organisation is set up and how a change is carried through it. Resourcing covers the job and the people in it. Development covers training and how teams work. Reward is empty by design: the catalogue holds no reward or job-evaluation framework, and the tile says so rather than hiding it. Engagement and culture covers why people perform and what the culture is. Analytics holds the calculators that work on declared figures.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Weighted summary
tools.what: Summarise scores with the design weights you supply, stating the weighting rule.
tools.need: the values you want to weigh and the weights you are declaring
tools.formula: Weighted mean = sum(weight x value) / sum(weight); design effect = (n - 1) / (n_effective - 1).
steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.
Read the weighted mean and the weighted standard deviation.
Read the effective sample size: how many unweighted observations your weights are worth.
common_mistakes: Entering the values and the weights in a different order.
Leaving the weight kind undeclared, so the two standard deviations cannot be told apart.
Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Training ROI
tools.what: Work out what a training or development spend returned, from the investment you declare and the gain you declare.
tools.need: everything the training cost, and the gain it produced net of that cost
tools.formula: ROI = net gain / total investment; annualised ROI = (1 + ROI)^(1/years) - 1.
steps: Enter everything the training cost: design, delivery, materials, cover, and the time people spend on it.
Enter the gain the training produced, net of that cost, over the period you are judging.
Declare the years only if the gain runs over more than one.
Read the return, then say what the gain was measured on and how it was established.
common_mistakes: Counting the whole gain as net gain when it already includes the training cost.
Leaving out the cost of the time people spend on the course.
Claiming a benefit from a reaction score and then calling it training ROI.
Comparing a training ROI with a discounted return: ROI ignores when the benefit arrives.

tools.label: Labour market tightness
tools.what: Read the real wage, the wage share of productivity and how tight the labour market is, from declared figures.
tools.need: the wage, the price index and productivity for one labour market, plus vacancies and unemployment
tools.formula: Real wage = nominal wage / (CPI / 100); wage share = real wage / labour productivity; tightness = vacancies / unemployed.
steps: Enter the nominal wage, the CPI and labour productivity for the same period and the same population.
Enter the vacancy count and the number of unemployed people for the labour market you are describing.
Read the real wage, the wage share of productivity and how tight the market is.
Say which labour market the figures describe: the method has no regional or sector breakdown.
common_mistakes: Mixing periods or populations between the wage, the price index and productivity.
Entering the CPI as a decimal instead of an index with a base of 100.
Reading a tight labour market as proof that a specific role is hard to fill.
Using the result as your organisation's own headcount gap: it describes the market, not your workforce.

tools.label: People programme cost-effectiveness
tools.what: Compare a people programme with a declared alternative on cost per unit of effect, with the effect you declare.
tools.need: the options, their costs and their effect on one scale you declare
tools.formula: ICER = (cost of the option - cost of the comparator) / (effect of the option - effect of the comparator).
steps: Enter the comparator option first: its name, its cost and its effect.
Enter each other option on the same cost basis and the same effect scale.
Declare the effect unit you use: people trained, roles filled, or any other single unit.
Read the incremental cost per unit of effect for each option, and check the dominance flags.
common_mistakes: Using different effect scales across options, which makes the ratio meaningless.
Putting the option you prefer first: the first option is the comparator.
Reading the ratio as a money value rather than a cost per unit of effect.
Adding a third option and expecting the earlier ratios to stay unchanged.

worksheets.label: Job Characteristics Model
worksheets.what: Record skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback for one role, with the evidence for each and the characteristics you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the role and describe the work as it is done now: the skills it needs, the piece of work it produces, what it contributes, what the person is free to decide, and how they hear how they are doing. The pipeline takes what you state and researches job-design evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Kirkpatrick training evaluation
worksheets.what: Record reaction, learning, behaviour and results for one training, with the baseline, the measure and the interval at each level.
worksheets.before: Name the training and describe what you know at each level: what participants said, what they could show afterwards, what changed at work, and what the organisation gained. The pipeline takes what you state and researches training-evaluation evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: AMO performance diagnosis
worksheets.what: Diagnose whether the constraint is ability, motivation or opportunity, with the evidence for each and the constraint you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the performance problem and describe it: what the work needs, what the people doing it will and will not do, and what stands in the way. The pipeline takes what you state and researches the evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Tuckman's team development stages
worksheets.what: Organise a discussion of forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, with the evidence you observe and the stages you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the team and describe what you have seen it do: how it started, what it argued about, what it agreed, how it worked once settled, and what ended it or changed its membership. The pipeline takes what you state and researches team-development evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Nine-box talent grid
worksheets.what: Declare the two axes, record who you place and why, and state the action the placements require.
worksheets.before: Name the group and declare your criteria for performance and for potential. State where each person you name sits and why. The development action each placement requires is yours to state: the pipeline leaves it to you.

worksheets.label: RACI responsibility matrix
worksheets.what: Assign R, A, C or I to each activity and role, with exactly one accountable role and at least one responsible role per activity.
worksheets.before: R does the work, A owns the outcome, C is consulted, I is informed. Every activity needs exactly one A and at least one R; write the letter first, then an optional note.

worksheets.label: Kotter's eight-step change model
worksheets.what: Record the eight steps - urgency, coalition, vision, communication, empowerment, short-term wins, consolidation and institutionalisation - with the evidence for each.
worksheets.before: Name the change and describe where it stands: what makes it urgent, who leads it, what the organisation is aiming at, how that reaches people, what stops them acting, what early result you can reach, and what would make it permanent. The pipeline takes what you state and researches change evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Organisational design review
worksheets.what: Check the fit between strategy, decision rights, structure, processes, people and incentives, and record where the fit breaks.
worksheets.before: Name the organisation and describe its six parts: what it is trying to achieve, who decides what, how the work is grouped, how it actually flows, the capability it needs and what it rewards people for. The pipeline takes what you state and researches design evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Competing Values Framework
worksheets.what: Read the culture through clan, adhocracy, market and hierarchy, with the survey or observation evidence behind each.
worksheets.before: Name the organisation or team and describe what you observe about it: how it looks after its people, how it treats experimentation, how it treats achievement and the customer, and how it is controlled. The pipeline takes what you state and researches culture evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: ADKAR readiness review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence behind each of the five ADKAR elements for one change programme, and audit the elements that have no evidence behind them.

worksheets.label: Lewin's three-stage change review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence for the three stages of one change programme and audit the stage the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: McKinsey 7-S alignment review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence across the seven elements of one organisation and record where the elements do not fit each other.

worksheets.label: Burke-Litwin organisational change review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Trace one change through the twelve elements of one organisation and audit the element the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: Galbraith star operating model review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence across the five elements of one operating model and audit the element that does not hold the others up.

worksheets.label: Theory of change with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Lay the causal links from inputs through activities and outputs to outcomes for one programme, and audit the links that rest on assumptions.

worksheets.label: Logic model with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Lay the inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes of one programme beside each other and audit the element the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: PDSA improvement cycle with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Record one cycle of a small test of change, from the plan and the prediction to what was studied and what was adopted.

worksheets.label: DMAIC improvement cycle with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Walk one process improvement through the five steps of DMAIC and audit the step the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: Mintzberg configuration review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read how one organisation is actually put together, part by part, and audit the part the evidence cannot settle.

tiles.label: Strategy and design
tiles.what: How the organisation is designed, how the strategy is set out, and how a change is carried through it.
tiles.need: The organisation, the strategy it has, and the change you are planning.

worksheets.label: Kotter's eight-step change model
worksheets.what: Record the eight steps - urgency, coalition, vision, communication, empowerment, short-term wins, consolidation and institutionalisation - with the evidence for each.
worksheets.before: Name the change and describe where it stands: what makes it urgent, who leads it, what the organisation is aiming at, how that reaches people, what stops them acting, what early result you can reach, and what would make it permanent. The pipeline takes what you state and researches change evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Organisational design review
worksheets.what: Check the fit between strategy, decision rights, structure, processes, people and incentives, and record where the fit breaks.
worksheets.before: Name the organisation and describe its six parts: what it is trying to achieve, who decides what, how the work is grouped, how it actually flows, the capability it needs and what it rewards people for. The pipeline takes what you state and researches design evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Lewin's three-stage change review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence for the three stages of one change programme and audit the stage the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: McKinsey 7-S alignment review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence across the seven elements of one organisation and record where the elements do not fit each other.

worksheets.label: Burke-Litwin organisational change review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Trace one change through the twelve elements of one organisation and audit the element the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: Galbraith star operating model review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence across the five elements of one operating model and audit the element that does not hold the others up.

worksheets.label: Theory of change with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Lay the causal links from inputs through activities and outputs to outcomes for one programme, and audit the links that rest on assumptions.

worksheets.label: Logic model with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Lay the inputs, activities, outputs and outcomes of one programme beside each other and audit the element the evidence cannot settle.

worksheets.label: Mintzberg configuration review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read how one organisation is actually put together, part by part, and audit the part the evidence cannot settle.

tiles.label: Resourcing
tiles.what: The job itself, the people who fill it, and who is responsible for what.
tiles.need: The role, the work it does and the people doing it.

worksheets.label: Job Characteristics Model
worksheets.what: Record skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback for one role, with the evidence for each and the characteristics you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the role and describe the work as it is done now: the skills it needs, the piece of work it produces, what it contributes, what the person is free to decide, and how they hear how they are doing. The pipeline takes what you state and researches job-design evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Nine-box talent grid
worksheets.what: Declare the two axes, record who you place and why, and state the action the placements require.
worksheets.before: Name the group and declare your criteria for performance and for potential. State where each person you name sits and why. The development action each placement requires is yours to state: the pipeline leaves it to you.

worksheets.label: RACI responsibility matrix
worksheets.what: Assign R, A, C or I to each activity and role, with exactly one accountable role and at least one responsible role per activity.
worksheets.before: R does the work, A owns the outcome, C is consulted, I is informed. Every activity needs exactly one A and at least one R; write the letter first, then an optional note.

tiles.label: Development
tiles.what: How people are trained and how teams develop, and how the work itself is improved.
tiles.need: The course, the team or the process you are reviewing.

worksheets.label: Kirkpatrick training evaluation
worksheets.what: Record reaction, learning, behaviour and results for one training, with the baseline, the measure and the interval at each level.
worksheets.before: Name the training and describe what you know at each level: what participants said, what they could show afterwards, what changed at work, and what the organisation gained. The pipeline takes what you state and researches training-evaluation evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Tuckman's team development stages
worksheets.what: Organise a discussion of forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning, with the evidence you observe and the stages you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the team and describe what you have seen it do: how it started, what it argued about, what it agreed, how it worked once settled, and what ended it or changed its membership. The pipeline takes what you state and researches team-development evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: ADKAR readiness review with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Read the evidence behind each of the five ADKAR elements for one change programme, and audit the elements that have no evidence behind them.

worksheets.label: PDSA improvement cycle with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Record one cycle of a small test of change, from the plan and the prediction to what was studied and what was adopted.

worksheets.label: DMAIC improvement cycle with an evidence audit
worksheets.what: Walk one process improvement through the five steps of DMAIC and audit the step the evidence cannot settle.

tiles.label: Reward
tiles.what: How pay, reward and job evaluation are set.
tiles.need: The pay structure and the roles it covers.
tiles.note: The catalogue holds no reward or job-evaluation framework, so this tile is empty by design and not by omission. It stays empty until the catalogue gains one.

tiles.label: Engagement and culture
tiles.what: Why people do or do not perform, and what the culture of the organisation is.
tiles.need: The performance problem or the culture you are reading.

worksheets.label: AMO performance diagnosis
worksheets.what: Diagnose whether the constraint is ability, motivation or opportunity, with the evidence for each and the constraint you cannot evidence named.
worksheets.before: Name the performance problem and describe it: what the work needs, what the people doing it will and will not do, and what stands in the way. The pipeline takes what you state and researches the evidence it can cite.

worksheets.label: Competing Values Framework
worksheets.what: Read the culture through clan, adhocracy, market and hierarchy, with the survey or observation evidence behind each.
worksheets.before: Name the organisation or team and describe what you observe about it: how it looks after its people, how it treats experimentation, how it treats achievement and the customer, and how it is controlled. The pipeline takes what you state and researches culture evidence it can cite.

tiles.label: Analytics
tiles.what: The declared-input calculators that work on people data: the statistics for a survey or a table of counts, and the money arithmetic for a training return, a labour market and a programme's cost.
tiles.need: The numbers you already hold, and the period they cover.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.

tools.label: Weighted summary
tools.what: Summarise scores with the design weights you supply, stating the weighting rule.
tools.need: the values you want to weigh and the weights you are declaring
tools.formula: Weighted mean = sum(weight x value) / sum(weight); design effect = (n - 1) / (n_effective - 1).
steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.
Read the weighted mean and the weighted standard deviation.
Read the effective sample size: how many unweighted observations your weights are worth.
common_mistakes: Entering the values and the weights in a different order.
Leaving the weight kind undeclared, so the two standard deviations cannot be told apart.
Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Training ROI
tools.what: Work out what a training or development spend returned, from the investment you declare and the gain you declare.
tools.need: everything the training cost, and the gain it produced net of that cost
tools.formula: ROI = net gain / total investment; annualised ROI = (1 + ROI)^(1/years) - 1.
steps: Enter everything the training cost: design, delivery, materials, cover, and the time people spend on it.
Enter the gain the training produced, net of that cost, over the period you are judging.
Declare the years only if the gain runs over more than one.
Read the return, then say what the gain was measured on and how it was established.
common_mistakes: Counting the whole gain as net gain when it already includes the training cost.
Leaving out the cost of the time people spend on the course.
Claiming a benefit from a reaction score and then calling it training ROI.
Comparing a training ROI with a discounted return: ROI ignores when the benefit arrives.

tools.label: Labour market tightness
tools.what: Read the real wage, the wage share of productivity and how tight the labour market is, from declared figures.
tools.need: the wage, the price index and productivity for one labour market, plus vacancies and unemployment
tools.formula: Real wage = nominal wage / (CPI / 100); wage share = real wage / labour productivity; tightness = vacancies / unemployed.
steps: Enter the nominal wage, the CPI and labour productivity for the same period and the same population.
Enter the vacancy count and the number of unemployed people for the labour market you are describing.
Read the real wage, the wage share of productivity and how tight the market is.
Say which labour market the figures describe: the method has no regional or sector breakdown.
common_mistakes: Mixing periods or populations between the wage, the price index and productivity.
Entering the CPI as a decimal instead of an index with a base of 100.
Reading a tight labour market as proof that a specific role is hard to fill.
Using the result as your organisation's own headcount gap: it describes the market, not your workforce.

tools.label: People programme cost-effectiveness
tools.what: Compare a people programme with a declared alternative on cost per unit of effect, with the effect you declare.
tools.need: the options, their costs and their effect on one scale you declare
tools.formula: ICER = (cost of the option - cost of the comparator) / (effect of the option - effect of the comparator).
steps: Enter the comparator option first: its name, its cost and its effect.
Enter each other option on the same cost basis and the same effect scale.
Declare the effect unit you use: people trained, roles filled, or any other single unit.
Read the incremental cost per unit of effect for each option, and check the dominance flags.
common_mistakes: Using different effect scales across options, which makes the ratio meaningless.
Putting the option you prefer first: the first option is the comparator.
Reading the ratio as a money value rather than a cost per unit of effect.
Adding a third option and expecting the earlier ratios to stay unchanged.

research.label: Research & statistics
research.summary: The cross-cutting method shelf: every statistical method the engine can run, linked from every subject.
start_steps: Describe the data: Descriptive statistics.
Compare groups: Welch two-sample t-test, Mann-Whitney U, One-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis.
Relate variables: Pearson or Spearman correlation, Linear regression or Logistic regression.
Check the design: Power and sample size, Multiple-comparison correction and Missing-data bounds.
does_not: It does not design the study, choose the hypothesis or clean the data for you.
It does not prove causality from observational data.
It does not replace a statistician for a complex or clustered design.
research.guidance: This is the cross-cutting method shelf. Start with the design and the data shape, then choose the test. Every output states its assumptions, its checks and what it cannot establish; a significant result is not a causal claim.

tools.label: Descriptive statistics
tools.what: Record the count, centre, spread and declared missing-value handling for one variable.
tools.need: the numbers you hold and the group they describe
tools.formula: Mean = sum of values / count; standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Spearman rank correlation
tools.what: Record the rank association between two variables without assuming a linear shape.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Linear regression (HC3)
tools.what: The same regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
tools.formula: The same OLS coefficients with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
steps: Fit the same model as OLS.
Read the robust standard errors and their tests.
Compare with the ordinary OLS errors to see whether heteroskedasticity mattered.
Keep the model specification fixed when comparing.
common_mistakes: Thinking robust errors fix a misspecified model.
Comparing robust errors with a different sample or specification.
Using HC3 as a substitute for checking outliers.
Reporting robust errors without saying which correction was used.

tools.label: Welch two-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare two group means without assuming equal variances.
tools.formula: t = (mean A - mean B) / standard error of the difference, without assuming equal variances.
steps: Check the two groups are independent.
Read the difference, the interval and the p-value together.
Report the effect size, not only significance.
common_mistakes: Treating a small p-value as a large effect.
Using a paired test for independent groups.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Mann-Whitney U test
tools.what: Compare two groups by rank when the distributional assumption is not met.

tools.label: One-way ANOVA
tools.what: Compare three or more group means and record the effect size and checks.
tools.formula: F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
steps: Check the groups are independent.
Read the F test and the effect size.
Use a post-hoc test before naming which groups differ.
common_mistakes: Running several t-tests instead of one ANOVA.
Naming the winning group from the omnibus test alone.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
tools.what: Compare three or more groups by rank, the non-parametric alternative to ANOVA.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Two-way ANOVA
tools.what: Record the two main effects and their interaction with the frozen checks.

tools.label: Post-hoc pairwise tests
tools.what: Compare group pairs after a significant omnibus test, with the correction declared.

tools.label: Multiple-comparison correction
tools.what: Correct a declared family of tests and show the adjusted decisions.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Missing-data bounds
tools.what: Bound how far the missing values could move the mean, without imputing them.
tools.formula: The mean is bounded by valuing every missing observation at the minimum and at the maximum observed value; the bound width shows how much the missing data could move it.
steps: Enter the observations you have, leaving missing values blank or marking their codes.
Declare the missing-data mechanism you believe applies; it is recorded, not verified.
Read the complete-case mean and the worst-case bounds.
Report the bound beside the estimate, not instead of it.
common_mistakes: Treating the bound as a confidence interval.
Assuming the missing values are random without evidence.
Dropping incomplete rows and reporting the mean as if nothing were missing.
Using a missing code as a real observation.

tools.label: Paired t-test
tools.what: Compare paired before/after measurements on the same units.

tools.label: One-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare a sample mean with a declared target.

tools.label: Logistic regression
tools.what: Fit a declared binary-outcome model and record coefficients and fit checks.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)

Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.

Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.

steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.

Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.

tiles.label: Describe the data
tiles.what: What one variable looks like before anything is tested: its centre, its spread, its shape, its missing entries, and the same summary when observations carry different weights.
tiles.need: The observations for one variable, and any declared missing codes or weights.

steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read the centre and spread together.
Look at the shape before using the mean alone.
common_mistakes: Reporting a mean for a heavily skewed variable without the median.
Ignoring missing values.
Confusing standard deviation with standard error.

tools.label: Weighted summary
tools.what: Summarise scores with the design weights you supply, stating the weighting rule.
tools.need: the values you want to weigh and the weights you are declaring
tools.formula: Weighted mean = sum(weight x value) / sum(weight); design effect = (n - 1) / (n_effective - 1).
steps: Enter one value per line and one weight per line, in the same order.
Declare the kind of weight: frequency, reliability or sampling.
Read the weighted mean and the weighted standard deviation.
Read the effective sample size: how many unweighted observations your weights are worth.
common_mistakes: Entering the values and the weights in a different order.
Leaving the weight kind undeclared, so the two standard deviations cannot be told apart.
Using reliability weights and then treating the result as a population average.
Expecting a confidence interval: this method summarises and does not test.

tiles.label: Compare groups
tiles.what: Whether two or more groups differ: Welch's t-test and its rank alternative, one-way and two-way ANOVA with Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square association, post-hoc pairwise tests, and paired and one-sample t-tests.
tiles.need: The observations named by group, or the counts in a contingency table.

tools.label: Welch two-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare two group means without assuming equal variances.
tools.formula: t = (mean A - mean B) / standard error of the difference, without assuming equal variances.
steps: Check the two groups are independent.
Read the difference, the interval and the p-value together.
Report the effect size, not only significance.
common_mistakes: Treating a small p-value as a large effect.
Using a paired test for independent groups.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Mann-Whitney U test
tools.what: Compare two groups by rank when the distributional assumption is not met.

tools.label: One-way ANOVA
tools.what: Compare three or more group means and record the effect size and checks.
tools.formula: F = between-group variance / within-group variance.
steps: Check the groups are independent.
Read the F test and the effect size.
Use a post-hoc test before naming which groups differ.
common_mistakes: Running several t-tests instead of one ANOVA.
Naming the winning group from the omnibus test alone.
Ignoring unequal variances.

tools.label: Kruskal-Wallis test
tools.what: Compare three or more groups by rank, the non-parametric alternative to ANOVA.

tools.label: Chi-square association
tools.what: Test whether two categorical variables are associated, with the expected-count checks.
tools.need: a two-way table of counts, and the categories in each direction
tools.formula: Chi-square = sum of (observed - expected)^2 / expected.
steps: Build the contingency table.
Check the expected counts.
Read the p-value and the effect size.
common_mistakes: Using chi-square with very small expected counts.
Reading causation into an association.
Ignoring the table's degrees of freedom.

tools.label: Two-way ANOVA
tools.what: Record the two main effects and their interaction with the frozen checks.

tools.label: Post-hoc pairwise tests
tools.what: Compare group pairs after a significant omnibus test, with the correction declared.

tools.label: Paired t-test
tools.what: Compare paired before/after measurements on the same units.

tools.label: One-sample t-test
tools.what: Compare a sample mean with a declared target.

tiles.label: Relate variables
tiles.what: Whether variables move together and how: Pearson and Spearman correlation, linear, robust and logistic regression with their diagnostics, and the trend forecast that follows a series over time.
tiles.need: Paired observations of the variables, or the series and the horizon to forecast.

tools.label: Pearson correlation
tools.what: Record the linear association between two variables with its sample size and checks.
tools.need: the two numeric variables you are relating, and the pairs you observed
tools.formula: r = covariance(x, y) / (standard deviation of x x standard deviation of y).
steps: Check both variables are numeric and paired.
Read r between minus one and one.
Inspect the scatter plot before trusting a linear summary.
common_mistakes: Reading causation into a correlation.
Ignoring an outlier that drives r.
Using Pearson for a clearly non-linear relationship.

tools.label: Spearman rank correlation
tools.what: Record the rank association between two variables without assuming a linear shape.

tools.label: Linear regression
tools.what: Fit a declared linear model and record coefficients, fit and diagnostics.
tools.need: the outcome, the predictors, and the observations you have for each
tools.formula: y = intercept + coefficient x x + error; the coefficients minimise the sum of squared errors.
steps: Check the sample size and missing values.
Read each coefficient with its standard error.
Check the fit and residual diagnostics.
State the assumptions and the claim ceiling.
common_mistakes: Reading a coefficient as a causal effect.
Ignoring heteroskedasticity or influential points.
Comparing R-squared across different dependent variables.

tools.label: Linear regression (HC3)
tools.what: The same regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
tools.formula: The same OLS coefficients with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors.
steps: Fit the same model as OLS.
Read the robust standard errors and their tests.
Compare with the ordinary OLS errors to see whether heteroskedasticity mattered.
Keep the model specification fixed when comparing.
common_mistakes: Thinking robust errors fix a misspecified model.
Comparing robust errors with a different sample or specification.
Using HC3 as a substitute for checking outliers.
Reporting robust errors without saying which correction was used.

tools.label: Logistic regression
tools.what: Fit a declared binary-outcome model and record coefficients and fit checks.

tools.label: Trend forecast
tools.what: Fit a trend to your own series and record the forecast periods and the range the result could fall in.
tools.need: a series in period order and the horizon
tools.formula: Fit y = a + bt to the series; the forecast extends the line and carries a prediction interval.
steps: Enter the series in order, one value per period.
Declare the horizon you want to forecast.
Read the trend, the forecast values and the interval.
Check the holdout error before trusting the extrapolation.
common_mistakes: Extrapolating far beyond the data without widening the interval.
Ignoring seasonality that a straight line cannot capture.
Reading a high R-squared as proof that the forecast is right.
Forecasting a series that changed regime.

tiles.label: Check the design
tiles.what: Whether the study could have found what it looked for: power and the minimum detectable effect, multiple-comparison correction, bounds under missing data, and the reliability of an instrument's items.
tiles.need: The effect you would want to detect and the sample, the p-values or tests you already ran, or the item responses.

tools.label: Multiple-comparison correction
tools.what: Correct a declared family of tests and show the adjusted decisions.

tools.label: Power and sample size
tools.what: Record the sample size or power implied by a declared effect and alpha.
tools.need: the size of the effect you are looking for and the number of observations
tools.formula: Power depends on the effect size, alpha, sample size and variability.
steps: Declare the effect size you care about.
Choose alpha and the desired power.
Read the required sample size or the detectable effect.
common_mistakes: Choosing the effect size after seeing the data.
Confusing power with the p-value.
Ignoring attrition and clustering.

tools.label: Missing-data bounds
tools.what: Bound how far the missing values could move the mean, without imputing them.
tools.formula: The mean is bounded by valuing every missing observation at the minimum and at the maximum observed value; the bound width shows how much the missing data could move it.
steps: Enter the observations you have, leaving missing values blank or marking their codes.
Declare the missing-data mechanism you believe applies; it is recorded, not verified.
Read the complete-case mean and the worst-case bounds.
Report the bound beside the estimate, not instead of it.
common_mistakes: Treating the bound as a confidence interval.
Assuming the missing values are random without evidence.
Dropping incomplete rows and reporting the mean as if nothing were missing.
Using a missing code as a real observation.

tools.label: Reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
tools.what: Check whether a set of survey items measures the same thing consistently, with the item and respondent counts stated.
tools.need: the items of your scale and the people who answered it
tools.formula: Cronbach's alpha = (k / (k - 1)) x (1 - sum of item variances / total variance), for k items.
steps: List the answers for every respondent to every survey item, keeping the same scale direction.
Check that higher scores mean the same thing on every item, reversing items where they do not.
Read alpha with the number of items and respondents beside it.
Report alpha as evidence about the instrument, not about the people who answered.
common_mistakes: Treating alpha as a measure of validity rather than internal consistency.
Reporting alpha without saying how many items and respondents it used.
Forgetting to reverse-code negatively worded items.
Assuming a high alpha means the scale measures one thing.
